policies.title: Code is Written for Humans First
policies.statement: Code is written for human readers first; any function must be understandable within 30 seconds, and comments explain WHY, never WHAT.
policies.rationale_summary: In a distributed team of 20–50 engineers, code is read tens of times for every time it is written.

policies.title: Quality is Built-In, Never Added Later
policies.statement: Quality is built in at the moment code is written, never deferred; a TODO without a tracked ticket and context is a defect.
policies.rationale_summary: Deferred quality is debt issued at predatory interest: unaddressed tech debt was one of the six founding pain points of this constitution.

policies.title: Consistency Enables Collaboration
policies.statement: All projects use identical tooling and conventions with zero project-level exceptions; conventions change only by amendment, for everyone.
policies.rationale_summary: Inconsistent standards across projects were a founding pain point: every project-specific convention is a tax on every engineer who moves between projects, and on every reviewer reading an unfamiliar repo.

policies.title: Architecture Decisions Are Intentional
policies.statement: System structure is the product of deliberate, recorded decisions; significant architectural choices require an ADR before merge.
policies.rationale_summary: Undocumented architecture is rediscovered at the worst possible time — by the next engineer, mid-incident, or during an audit.

policies.title: Security is Everybody's Responsibility
policies.statement: Security defects block merge regardless of author or deadline; only a named human security lead may override a CRITICAL finding, recorded in the PR.
policies.rationale_summary: Security vulnerabilities reaching production was a founding pain point of this constitution.

policies.title: Naming Conventions
policies.statement: Identifiers follow the constitution's naming table: camelCase variables/functions, PascalCase types without I-prefix, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE constants, is/has/can booleans, kebab-case files.
policies.rationale_summary: Names are the primary interface between code and reader.

policies.title: Formatting via Prettier
policies.statement: All code is formatted by Prettier with the shared config (2-space, 100-char, single quotes, semicolons, ES5 trailing commas); formatting is never manual.
policies.rationale_summary: Every minute spent formatting — or arguing about formatting in review — is waste, and review bottlenecks were a founding pain point.

policies.title: Prohibition of the any Type
policies.statement: The `any` type is prohibited. Use `unknown` with type narrowing.
policies.rationale_summary: any silently disables TypeScript's type checking for that value and everything it touches, defeating the purpose of strict mode and allowing type errors to reach production.

policies.title: Explicit Return Types on Exported Functions
policies.statement: Every exported function declares its return type explicitly; a public signature is a written contract, not an inference.
policies.rationale_summary: Inferred return types on public surfaces make the contract whatever the implementation happens to return: an internal refactor silently changes the API and the breakage surfaces in distant consumers, attributed to the wrong commit.

policies.title: Import Ordering
policies.statement: Imports are grouped stdlib → third-party → local, alphabetized within groups, enforced by ESLint — never maintained by hand.
policies.rationale_summary: A file's imports are its dependency manifest.

policies.title: Function Size and Responsibility
policies.statement: Functions do one thing with depth of abstraction as the goal; complexity ≤5 and ~40 lines are advisory review thresholds, fragmenting a coherent responsibility to satisfy a number is itself a violation, and meaningful literals are named constants.
policies.rationale_summary: Complexity, not length, is what defeats readers: a linear 35-line function can pass the 30-second test (POL-1.1) while a "compliant" web of six 8-line fragments fails it — over-decomposition produces shallow interfaces and entanglement, where understanding one method requires reading several (Ousterhout, Martin–Ousterhout debate 2024–25).

policies.title: Test-First Development
policies.statement: Tests are written before implementation per Canon TDD — test list, one failing test at a time, red-green-refactor — and no agent or engineer may delete, skip, or weaken a failing test to achieve green.
policies.rationale_summary: A test written after the implementation tends to assert what the code does, not what it should do — it inherits the implementation's bugs as expectations.

policies.title: Coverage Floors
policies.statement: CI enforces coverage floors — 80% business logic, 100% utilities, 70% controllers — and they may not be lowered to make a build pass.
policies.rationale_summary: Low test coverage was a founding pain point: untested paths are where production incidents live.

policies.title: Test Structure
policies.statement: Tests follow Arrange-Act-Assert with one action per test, named 'should <expectation> when <scenario>'.
policies.rationale_summary: Tests are the executable specification of the system — they are read most often at the worst time: when they fail, in CI, by someone who didn't write them.

policies.title: Test Isolation
policies.statement: Unit tests mock all external dependencies, complete in under one second, and never depend on another test's execution or ordering.
policies.rationale_summary: Tests that touch real dependencies are slow, flaky, and ambiguous: a failure might mean broken code, a down service, or a dirty database, and engineers learn to re-run instead of investigate — at which point the suite's signal is dead.

policies.title: No Skipped or Hollow Tests
policies.statement: No .skip without a tracked ticket; every test must assert on behavior and be able to fail when that behavior breaks.
policies.rationale_summary: A skipped test is a known blind spot; without a ticket it is a permanent one that silently exempts a behavior from the safety net while still appearing in the suite.

policies.title: Mutation Testing Verifies Test Effectiveness
policies.statement: Test effectiveness is verified by mutation testing; AI-generated tests are accepted only when they kill mutants beyond the existing suite, and mutation-score baselines ratchet upward, never down.
policies.rationale_summary: Coverage proves code ran; mutation score proves tests notice when code breaks.

policies.title: Layered Architecture
policies.statement: Applications are organized by business domain first with the four layers inside each domain, dependencies pointing downward, cross-domain access through public interfaces only, and a modular-monolith default — service extraction requires an ADR meeting a documented criterion.
policies.rationale_summary: Layering is what keeps change local.

policies.title: SOLID Compliance
policies.statement: All modules comply with SOLID, verified by the one-line tests — one reason to change, open to extension, substitutable subtypes, lean interfaces, depend on abstractions.
policies.rationale_summary: SOLID is the difference between a system that absorbs change and one that shatters under it.

policies.title: No Circular Dependencies
policies.statement: Circular dependencies are prohibited at any distance; import/no-cycle is a build error, and shared concepts are extracted into a module beneath both.
policies.rationale_summary: A cycle means neither module can be understood, tested, loaded, or replaced without the other — they are one module wearing two names, and every module in the cycle inherits the union of all their reasons to change.

policies.title: Sanctioned Patterns
policies.statement: DI, Repository, Factory, and Strategy are required in their defined situations; novel patterns require an ADR explaining why the sanctioned set was insufficient.
policies.rationale_summary: A small sanctioned vocabulary means every engineer and agent reads every codebase fluently: a *Repository always means the same thing, in every project (POL-1.3 applied to design).

policies.title: ADR Requirement
policies.statement: Significant structural decisions are recorded as an ADR in docs/adr/ before the implementing change merges.
policies.rationale_summary: The most expensive question in a legacy system is "can we change this?" — and it's expensive precisely because nobody recorded why it is the way it is.

policies.title: Resilience Patterns
policies.statement: Every network-boundary call has explicit timeouts, bounded exponential-backoff-with-jitter retries, idempotency keys on retryable mutations, and circuit breakers with a defined degraded mode.
policies.rationale_summary: Distributed failure is a certainty, not an edge case — AWS's Well-Architected reliability pillar codifies designing for recovery as first-class practice.

policies.title: Universal Input Validation
policies.statement: All external data is validated at the boundary with allowlist validation before use; failing data is rejected, never sanitized into acceptability.
policies.rationale_summary: Nearly every injection class — SQL, XSS, command, path traversal, deserialization — begins as unvalidated external data reaching code that trusts it.

policies.title: Parameterized Queries Only
policies.statement: Queries are built exclusively with parameterized statements; concatenating or interpolating any runtime value into query text is prohibited.
policies.rationale_summary: SQL injection has been the most exploited vulnerability class for over two decades, and every instance begins with one engineer concatenating "just this one" value.

policies.title: Secrets Never in Code
policies.statement: Secrets never appear in code, committed config, images, or logs — runtime env/secret manager only; a committed secret is rotated, not removed.
policies.rationale_summary: Version control never forgets: a secret committed once survives in history through every clone, fork, and backup, beyond the reach of any later deletion.

policies.title: Established Auth Frameworks Only
policies.statement: Auth uses established frameworks (OAuth2/OIDC, vetted JWT, SAML) exclusively; custom cryptography, session, or token schemes are categorically prohibited.
policies.rationale_summary: Cryptographic and auth code fails silently: it works perfectly in every demo and falls only to an adversary — timing side channels, padding oracles, token confusion, session fixation — failure modes that don't appear in tests (so POL-3.2 coverage cannot save you) and that took the field decades to discover.

policies.title: Dependency Hygiene
policies.statement: Dependencies are scanned weekly and per-PR; criticals are patched within 24 hours, lockfiles are committed, and versions are pinned exactly.
policies.rationale_summary: A modern Node.js application is mostly other people's code — typically hundreds of transitive packages, each a potential entry point.

policies.title: Encryption Standards
policies.statement: Data in transit uses TLS 1.2+ everywhere including internal traffic; sensitive data at rest is encrypted to current standards with managed keys.
policies.rationale_summary: Plaintext transport makes every network segment a wiretap point; "internal" networks stop being a defense the moment any single host, container, or VPC peering is compromised — which is why zero-trust practice encrypts everywhere, not just at the edge.

policies.title: Two-Approval Review
policies.statement: Every merge requires two approvals including one domain expert; authors never approve their own changes.
policies.rationale_summary: A single reviewer under deadline pressure converges on rubber-stamping; two reviewers with one required domain expert keep the review honest and catch the class of defects only context can see — a correct-looking change that violates a domain invariant.

policies.title: Quality Gates Are Inviolable
policies.statement: No change merges unless lint, type-check, tests, coverage, format, and security gates are all green; no override path exists for anyone.
policies.rationale_summary: A gate with an override path is a suggestion, and every suggestion loses to a deadline eventually.

policies.title: Public API Documentation
policies.statement: Every public function carries JSDoc with description, @param, @returns, @throws, and an @example for non-trivial surfaces.
policies.rationale_summary: A public function's signature says what types it takes; only its documentation says what it *means* — units, invariants, side effects, failure modes.

policies.title: Comments Explain WHY
policies.statement: Interface comments are part of the abstraction and WHY comments capture what code cannot express; a missing comment costs more than an imperfect one, while comments restating the implementation remain prohibited.
policies.rationale_summary: Code states WHAT perfectly and WHY not at all — intent, constraint, and context exist only in the author's head unless written down, and they are precisely what the next maintainer (or AI agent) needs before safely changing anything.

policies.title: Docs Travel With Code
policies.statement: Documentation is updated in the same PR as the change it describes; a behavior change leaving stale docs is incomplete and must not merge.
policies.rationale_summary: Documentation updated "later" is documentation updated never — the context evaporates the moment the PR merges and the author moves on.

policies.title: Human Accountability
policies.statement: A human engineer owns every merged line regardless of how it was produced; AI assists, humans approve, and 'the AI wrote it' is never a defense.
policies.rationale_summary: Accountability is what keeps quality real when generation becomes cheap.

policies.title: IP and Data Protection
policies.statement: No PII, secrets, payment/health data, client-confidential material, or proprietary algorithms may be sent to AI tools outside the approved list.
policies.rationale_summary: A prompt is an outbound data transfer: anything pasted into an AI tool leaves the organization's control and may be retained, logged, or used for training under terms we never reviewed.

policies.title: AI Audit Trail
policies.statement: AI involvement is disclosed at the point of record: [Claude-assisted] commit tag and the PR's AI Assistance section describing what was generated and what was verified.
policies.rationale_summary: Provenance enables every downstream safeguard.

policies.title: Identical Standards for AI Code
policies.statement: AI-generated code meets every constitutional standard with no relaxation; review verifies, never assumes — plausibility is not correctness.
policies.rationale_summary: AI output is optimized to look right — that is precisely what makes it dangerous to review casually.

policies.title: Mandatory Escalation on Uncertainty
policies.statement: On ambiguous requirements, lasting architectural choices, or unresolved security questions, agents stop and ask — guessing is prohibited even when the guess is correct.
policies.rationale_summary: Agents fail differently from humans: a human carrying an assumption mentions it at standup; an agent compiles it into the system, invisibly and at scale.

policies.title: AI-Era Code-Health Metrics
policies.statement: Projects track duplication, churn, and moved-vs-copied ratios per release; sustained regression is ticketed, actionable technical debt — and metrics are never individual performance measures.
policies.rationale_summary: AI generation makes duplicating code cheaper than abstracting it, and the industry-scale result is measured: across 211M changed lines (2020–2024), copy-pasted code rose from 8.3% to 12.3% of changes while moved/refactored code collapsed from 25% to under 10% — copy/paste exceeded refactoring for the first time on record (GitClear 2025).

policies.title: Acceptance Criteria Before Implementation
policies.statement: No implementation begins without written acceptance criteria defining observable behaviors, in-scope edge cases, and verification.
policies.rationale_summary: Undefined "done" is how the same feature gets built three times: once as the engineer imagined it, once as the PM meant it, once as the client needed it.

policies.title: Business Rules Are Documented and Cited
policies.statement: Every implemented business rule cites its documented source at the implementation site and in its covering test.
policies.rationale_summary: Uncited domain logic becomes archaeology: five years later, nobody knows whether if (days > 90) writeOff() is a regulation, a client preference, or a bug that shipped — so nobody dares change it, and nobody can verify it's still correct.

policies.title: Regulatory Mapping
policies.statement: Regulated projects maintain a compliance map from each requirement to the code and controls satisfying it, updated in the same PR as changes to mapped paths.
policies.rationale_summary: Compliance that lives in engineers' heads fails exactly when tested — at audit time and at incident time, both of which demand evidence, not assurance.

policies.title: Scope Discipline
policies.statement: Changes outside agreed scope require explicit Product Owner sign-off before implementation; adjacent improvements are ticketed, not smuggled.
policies.rationale_summary: Scope creep is invisible until it isn't: each "small extra" seems free, but it widens the review surface (raising the odds defects hide in the unrequested parts), invalidates estimates, and ships behavior no stakeholder agreed to — which in client work can mean contractual exposure.

policies.title: Infrastructure as Code
policies.statement: All infrastructure is defined in version-controlled code and changed only through reviewed commits; console-clicked resources are prohibited.
policies.rationale_summary: Hand-built infrastructure is unreproducible by definition: when the region fails or the account must be rebuilt, the click sequence that created production exists nowhere.

policies.title: Deployment Safety
policies.statement: Every deployment is reversible with the rollback documented before release; a deploy without a rollback plan does not proceed.
policies.rationale_summary: Every deploy is a hypothesis; rollback is the safety net that makes shipping frequently rational.

policies.title: Cost Impact Assessment
policies.statement: Changes with material cost impact include a PR cost estimate and FinOps review; all cloud resources carry attribution tags; cost never overrides security.
policies.rationale_summary: Cloud spend is the rare cost that engineers commit in code and finance discovers on an invoice — a single misjudged instance class or unbounded log retention compounds silently at 730 hours a month.

policies.title: License Compliance
policies.statement: Every dependency license (including transitives) is evaluated before adoption; copyleft and source-available licenses require human legal sign-off.
policies.rationale_summary: A license is a contract accepted by npm install, and in client- delivery work the exposure is double: copyleft obligations can attach to the *client's* proprietary codebase, converting a free library into a legal incident and a contractual breach.

policies.title: Service-Level Objectives
policies.statement: Every production service has documented SLOs with measured SLIs, signed off by product, development, and operations, with named authors, approvers, and review dates.
policies.rationale_summary: Reliability undefined is reliability unfalsifiable: without a target, every incident debate is opinion versus opinion.

policies.title: Error-Budget Policy
policies.statement: Exhausting the four-week error budget halts feature releases — only P0 and security fixes ship — and any incident consuming over 20% of the budget mandates a postmortem with a P0 root-cause action item.
policies.rationale_summary: The error budget converts the reliability-versus-velocity argument from a per-incident negotiation into a pre-agreed contract — exactly the move this constitution makes for quality gates (POL-6.2).

policies.title: Failure-Injection and Recovery Testing
policies.statement: Rollback, failover, restore, and degraded modes are exercised through quarterly failure-injection or game days; an untested recovery procedure is assumed broken.
policies.rationale_summary: A rollback document that has never run is documentation of hope: backups that were never restored, failovers that were never failed, degraded modes that were never degraded — each is discovered broken at the only moment it matters.

policies.title: Spec-Driven Agent Work
policies.statement: Substantial agent work proceeds from a reviewed written spec or plan that names the laws bearing on the work; agents do not begin substantial implementation without one.
policies.rationale_summary: Agents that jump straight to code solve the wrong problem confidently — at generation speed.

policies.title: Verifiable Completion
policies.statement: Every agent task defines a runnable check before implementation; the agent iterates until it passes and presents the evidence — completion claims without evidence are presumed unverified.
policies.rationale_summary: An agent without a runnable check stops when the work *looks* done — and plausible-looking is exactly what generated output is optimized for (POL-7.4).

policies.title: Agent Sandboxing and Permissions
policies.statement: Autonomous agent runs require BOTH filesystem and network isolation plus an explicit tool allowlist; agents never carry credentials beyond the task's needs, with prompt injection as the default threat model.
policies.rationale_summary: A coding agent is a code-execution surface whose instructions can arrive from anything it reads — issues, web pages, dependency READMEs.

policies.title: Steering Files Are Governed Artifacts
policies.statement: Steering files are code — version-controlled, PR-reviewed, concise, and pruned; always-rules become hooks or gates, not prose; projects ship both CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md.
policies.rationale_summary: Steering files are the constitution's delivery mechanism into every agent session — and they fail by accretion: Anthropic's verified guidance warns "bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions," and prescribes treating the file "like code: review it when things go wrong, prune it regularly, and test changes by observing whether the agent's behavior actually shifts." The hooks-over-prose rule exists because steering text is advisory by nature — a rule that must never be violated belongs in a mechanism that cannot be ignored (POL-6.2's logic applied to agents).

policies.title: Fresh-Context Review
policies.statement: Agent work is reviewed by a context that did not produce it; the implementing context never grades its own work and never deletes or weakens a failing check to reach green.
policies.rationale_summary: A context that produced a change carries the reasoning that produced its bugs: Anthropic's verified guidance — "a fresh context improves code review since Claude won't be biased toward code it just wrote" — is the agent-era restatement of why authors don't approve their own PRs (POL-6.1).

policies.title: Defined Workflows
policies.statement: Nontrivial work proceeds under a declared workflow whose stages, roles, and gates govern agents and humans alike; deviations on non-hard stages are permitted but recorded, and hard stages are never overridable.
policies.rationale_summary: Process that lives in memory fails exactly like undocumented architecture (POL-1.4) and unrecorded amendments: invisibly, then expensively — security review happens when someone remembers, and "did QA see this?" is answered by recollection.
